releases.name: v0.3.6 — Defects in moved code and unknown intent
releases.body:
# Azure DevOps PR Review for OpenCode — 0.3.6

This release changes two reviewer rules that kept real defects out of the
findings: one for code a pull request moves unchanged, and one for behavior
that might be intended. Settings, commands, comment previews, adjustments and
publication work as in 0.3.5, and the tested host stays OpenCode 2.2.4.

## What changed

- **Defects in moved code are filed.** A correctness or security defect on
  lines the PR adds or moves is filed even when the base commit had the same
  code elsewhere, such as a function moved to a new file. The finding says
  that the PR carries the defect over and shows where the base commit had it.
  Unrelated pre-existing issues still stay out.
- **A possible intention no longer keeps a defect out.** When behavior would be
  a defect unless the author meant it, and nothing in the code, tests,
  documentation or PR text says whether they did, reviewers file a low finding
  whose summary asks whether the author meant it and whose suggested fix asks
  them to confirm or document the intent. Low findings get no inline comment,
  so the question appears in the summary index.
- **The verifier no longer rejects for either reason.** Neither a possible
  intention nor identical base code refutes a finding. When only the author's
  intent would settle a verified behavior, the verifier confirms the finding
  with a summary and a suggestion that ask the author.

`/pr-review`, `/pr-deep` and `/pr-quick` share the reviewer rules; `/pr-quick`
has no verifier. Publication is unchanged: inline comments go to high and
medium findings, so the low questions about intent stay in the summary index.

## Measured effect

Both rules came from a run of Martian's Code Review Bench: among the expected
issues that no run had posted were defects in moved code and a finding
rejected as possibly intended. The wording was written after reading three of
them. In a local scoring run on the benchmark's 50 pull requests, with
`/pr-deep` and Claude Opus 5.5 at medium effort, recall rose from 65.2% to
67.7% and F2 from 51.6 to 53.2, with precision about the same.

Because the wording was written from that benchmark, 0.3.5 and 0.3.6 also
reviewed the 25 pull requests of the public
[ReviewBench](https://github.com/review-bench/ReviewBench) test set, which was
not used to write it, through a local fixture of the Azure DevOps API. Both were
scored with ReviewBench's judging pipeline and Claude Sonnet 5, the model that
judges its leaderboard. We ran the pipeline ourselves, so this is not a
leaderboard result:

| `/pr-deep`, Claude Opus 5.5 | Issues found (recall) | Findings judged valid | High and medium found | Inline decisions (F1) |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0.3.5 | 35.5% | 95.6% | 55.3% | 70.0 |
| 0.3.6 | 39.5% | 96.5% | 55.3% | 65.5 |

None of the four measures fell by more than the run-to-run variation allowed
for in advance. Inline decisions, the agreement with the judge on which
findings deserve an inline comment, fell because more findings the judge rated
medium or high were labeled low, 8 of them questions about intent, which the
new rule rates low. A local judge scored the same runs and a pair with
GPT-6.1 Sol: with Sol all four measures rose slightly, and with Claude Opus 5.5
it rated 2.4 points fewer of 0.3.6's findings valid, more than allowed. The
[validation record](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.6/docs/VALIDATION.md#defects-in-moved-code-and-unknown-intent-2026-11-09)
describes the method, both judges' results and the limits.

## Installation

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.6
```

Alternatively, install the same release from Git:

```sh
opencode plugin add 'github:WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2#v0.3.6'
```

Add only one of them. Follow the
[quickstart](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.6/docs/QUICKSTART.md)
for a private PAT file, `/pr-setup`, a service restar

releases.name: v0.3.5 — Severity from harm and realistic use
releases.body:
# Azure DevOps PR Review for OpenCode — 0.3.5

This release changes how reviewers set severity. A finding's severity now says
how much it matters to fix it before the change merges, judged from the harm
the evidence shows and how often realistic use reaches it. Settings, commands,
comment previews, adjustments and publication work as in 0.3.4, and the tested
host stays OpenCode 2.2.4.

## What changed

- **Severity says how much fixing matters before the merge.**
  - **high** (must fix before merging): realistic use leaves a core function
    or what the change is for not working, or causes serious harm: a security
    breach, data people keep lost, corrupted or exposed, or results people act
    on that are silently wrong.
  - **medium** (should fix in this change): realistic use hits a failure that
    people notice and recover from, such as an error or wrong result for some
    valid inputs, a broken secondary path or a failing test or build, or a rare
    trigger causes serious harm.
  - **low** (can wait): anything else, such as a recoverable failure that only
    a rare trigger reaches, or a finding with no effect on behavior
    (duplication, naming, a stale comment, a missing test for working code).

  Reviewers judge severity from the harm their evidence shows and how often
  realistic use reaches it, not from their confidence, the size of the fix or
  the kind of issue. Realistic use means ordinary inputs, common
  configurations and deployments, failures that dependencies routinely produce
  (a dropped connection, an error from a remote service), concurrent use where
  the code runs concurrently and, at a security boundary, anyone who can reach
  it. A rare trigger lowers a finding's severity; it does not keep a defect out
  of the findings.
- **Gaps are rated by their effect.** In 0.3.4 concrete gaps were usually low.
  Now a document or example is rated by what following it does, shipped
  configuration like code, and a missing or ineffective test is low unless the
  test is what the change delivers. When a missing test hides a defect in the
  change, the defect is reported with its own severity, and its suggested fix
  names the test that would catch it.
- **The verifier sets the final severity.** It sets each confirmed finding's
  severity from the harm and trigger it verified: the reviewer's severity is a
  claim like the rest, raised or lowered as the evidence requires, with the
  reason. `/pr-quick` reviewers use the same scale for their own checks.
- **Each rule is stated once.** The reviewer instructions no longer repeat
  shared rules in the role prompts, and the shared tool guidance leaves what
  each tool returns to the tools' own descriptions.

Publication is unchanged: inline comments go to high and medium findings, and
low findings stay in the summary index. With gpt-6.1-sol, reviews label many
more findings high and slightly fewer low, so slightly more findings get an
inline comment. `/pr-review`, `/pr-deep` and `/pr-quick` share these rules.

## Measured effect

Before release, the new instructions were compared with those of 0.3.4 on the
public [ReviewBench](https://github.com/review-bench/ReviewBench) test set,
served to OpenCode 2.2.4 through a local fixture of the Azure DevOps API and
scored with the benchmark's matcher and classifier rubric by Claude Opus
subagents rather than its official judge. Each finding's severity was compared
with the severity the judges gave the same issue, and two runs of the same
instructions measured how much results vary between runs. The comparison shows
the direction of the change, not a leaderboard result:

- With `/pr-deep` and gpt-6.1-sol, many more of the issues the judges rated
  high were labeled high, while the share of high labels that the judges also
  rated high stayed about the same. Fewer findings that deserve an inline
  comment were labeled low.

  variation between runs, an

releases.name: v0.3.4 — Concrete gaps and one finding per place
releases.body:
# Azure DevOps PR Review for OpenCode — 0.3.4

This release changes what reviewers report. Concrete gaps the change leaves,
such as an untested change or a document that now contradicts the code, become
findings, and a mistake repeated in several places is reported at each place
that needs its own fix. Settings, commands, comment previews, adjustments and
publication work as in 0.3.3, and the tested host stays OpenCode 2.2.4.

## What changed

- **Concrete gaps are findings.** Reviewers file, usually as low: a changed or
  added behavior that no test would catch where the project already tests
  comparable code (naming the missing case and the tests it belongs with), a
  test that cannot fail or checks the wrong thing, a comment, document,
  example, schema or configuration that now contradicts the code, and
  duplicated, dead, misleading or inconsistent code the change introduces.
  These used to appear only as advice in the report. Design trade-offs and
  general advice without a specific defect or location still go to the report
  and the summary's improvement suggestions.
- **One finding per place that needs its own fix.** When the same mistake is
  written separately in several functions, files or routes, for example three
  routes that each build a URL from the internal request origin, each place is
  its own finding at its own lines, with the sibling places in its evidence.
  Reviewers check their other assigned files for the same mistake. One wrong
  piece of shared code is still one finding at that code.
- **Identical copies count once per reviewer.** A template, example, document
  or vendored file repeated with identical content in several directories is
  one place among one reviewer's assigned files: one finding at one copy that
  lists the other copies. A large PR is reviewed in shards cut by path, so
  copies in different shards can each produce a finding. Files whose content
  differs, such as each package's own manifest, stay separate places.

Publication is unchanged: inline comments go to high and medium findings, and
low findings stay in the summary index. A review therefore shows more low
findings in the summary and, for a repeated high or medium mistake, one inline
comment at each place. `/pr-review`, `/pr-deep` and `/pr-quick` share these
rules.

## Measured effect

Before release, the new instructions were compared with 0.3.3 on the public
[ReviewBench](https://github.com/review-bench/ReviewBench) test set, served to
OpenCode 2.2.4 through a local fixture of the Azure DevOps API and scored with
the benchmark's matcher and classifier rubric by Claude Opus subagents rather
than its official judge. The comparison shows the direction of the change, not
a leaderboard result:

- With `/pr-deep` and gpt-6.1-sol, reviews matched more of the high- and
  medium-severity reference issues, including high ones. A mistake repeated in
  several routes was reported, and matched, at each route.
- Reviews produce more findings, mostly low, which stay in the summary index,
  and take somewhat longer; the share of findings judged valid stayed about the
  same.
- With `/pr-review` and gpt-6-luna, reviews matched slightly more, within the
  variation between runs.

The
[validation record](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.4/docs/VALIDATION.md)
describes the method and its limits.

## Installation

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.4
```

Alternatively, install the same release from Git:

```sh
opencode plugin add 'github:WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2#v0.3.4'
```

Add only one of them. Follow the
[quickstart](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.4/docs/QUICKSTART.md)
for a private PAT file, `/pr-setup`, a service restart and the first review.

releases.name: v0.3.3 — Tested with OpenCode 2.2.4, used-up limits stop at once
releases.body:
# Azure DevOps PR Review for OpenCode — 0.3.3

This release moves the tested host to OpenCode 2.2.4, stops at once when a
model's usage or spend limit is used up, and shows the OpenCode version in
`/pr-check` instead of a notice on every receipt. Reviews, comment previews,
adjustments and publication work as in 0.3.2.

## What changed

- **Tested with OpenCode 2.2.4.** AZPR is validated with OpenCode CLI 2.2.4
  instead of 2.1.4. The runtime needed no change: with the same fake provider,
  a review sends byte-identical model requests on both hosts. OpenCode 2.2.x
  offers new tools to every agent, such as image generation when a provider has
  an image model; private reviewers still see only AZPR's tools and the native
  read tools.
- **OpenCode version in `/pr-check`.** A new OpenCode row names the host
  version and is a WARNING when it is not the tested one; reviews still run,
  and AZPR still refuses to start if OpenCode lacks something it needs.
  Receipts no longer end with a host notice after every OpenCode update.
- **Used-up limits stop at once.** When a model's usage or spend limit is used
  up, AZPR refuses OpenCode's retries, starts no new session, and the receipt
  names the limit. Besides the provider quota and the OpenCode free-model
  limit, this covers the ChatGPT and OpenCode Go usage limits that OpenCode
  2.2.3 reports and OpenCode's spend limits; a used-up ChatGPT limit was
  previously retried as a rate limit.
- **Fewer host events.** AZPR subscribes only to the session events that show
  a review progressing; OpenCode 2.2.0 and later deliver no others.
- **Proxies.** OpenCode 2.2.4 always adds `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` and `::1`
  to `NO_PROXY`, and Bun honours `NO_PROXY` even for `azure.proxy`. Azure
  DevOps requests are unaffected; the
  [company-network guide](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.3/docs/ENTERPRISE.md#company-networks)
  now says to keep `dev.azure.com` out of `NO_PROXY` when it must use the
  proxy.

## Upgrading OpenCode

OpenCode 2.2.0 and later migrate OpenCode's database when they first start,
and the migration cannot be undone. Stop the service and back up the database
before installing 2.2.4:

```sh
opencode service stop
mkdir -p ~/opencode-db-backup && cp -p ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db* ~/opencode-db-backup/
npm install -g @opencode/cli@2.2.4
opencode service start
```

Use `sudo` for the global install if your npm prefix needs it. To go back,
stop the service, reinstall the previous OpenCode and restore the backup.
AZPR 0.3.3 also runs on OpenCode 2.1.4 (`/pr-check` then shows the OpenCode
WARNING row), so the two upgrades can happen in either order.

## Installation

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.3
```

Alternatively, install the same release from Git:

```sh
opencode plugin add 'github:WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2#v0.3.3'
```

Add only one of them. Follow the
[quickstart](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.3/docs/QUICKSTART.md)
for a private PAT file, `/pr-setup`, a service restart and the first review.

## Upgrading AZPR

For an entry that `opencode plugin add` created, add 0.3.3 and remove the
previous version only when the download succeeded. Replace `PREVIOUS_VERSION`
with the version in your `plugins` entry, such as 0.3.2:

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.3 &&
  opencode plugin remove opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@PREVIOUS_VERSION
```

Run them when no AZPR command is running: OpenCode 2.1.4 and 2.2.4 switch the
running service to 0.3.3 within seconds, without a restart, and
`opencode plugin list` should then show a single `azpr` row with 0.3.3. Running
only the first command leaves the previous version running. For an entry with
options, change only its `package` value; the OpenCode service then downloads
0.3.3 with its own network settings. See
[upgrading](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2

releases.name: v0.3.2 — Results first, precise receipts, smaller npm package
releases.body:
# Azure DevOps PR Review for OpenCode — 0.3.2

This release shows AZPR's actual Azure DevOps output at the top of the README,
states the COMPLETE status more precisely in receipts, and slims the npm
package to the runtime. Reviews, comment previews, adjustments and publication
work as in 0.3.1.

## What changed

- **See the output first.** The README opens with an actual inline comment on
  a dedicated test PR, shown with its code context, and the complete PR summary
  from the same review. The first-review steps follow, then the 15-second
  recording of adjusting findings and publishing. The
  [demo](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.2/docs/DEMO.md#actual-azure-devops-comments)
  records the capture run and its editing, and lists the pictured comments as
  text.
- **Precise status.** COMPLETE in a receipt now means that no source-commit
  change was detected. When the final version recheck itself fails, the review
  stays COMPLETE and its report lists a warning; publication still rechecks
  that the PR is active and its source commit is unchanged before posting.
- **Smaller npm package.** The package holds the runtime (`server.js` and
  `src/`), the README, the changelog and the license: 32 files and about 170 KB
  instead of 76 files and 1.35 MB. Documentation, media, installers and the
  settings example and schema remain in the repository and the source archive,
  and npmjs.com shows the README's links and images from GitHub.
- **Documentation.** The README and the architecture guide list the commands
  that answer directly instead of starting a background run, and the README
  and the commenting guide state that repeating the saved adjustments plans
  nothing.

## Installation

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.2
```

Alternatively, install the same release from Git:

```sh
opencode plugin add 'github:WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2#v0.3.2'
```

Add only one of them. Follow the
[quickstart](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.2/docs/QUICKSTART.md)
for a private PAT file, `/pr-setup`, a service restart and the first review.

## Upgrading

For an entry that `opencode plugin add` created, add 0.3.2 and remove the
previous version only when the download succeeded. Replace `PREVIOUS_VERSION`
with the version in your `plugins` entry, such as 0.3.1:

```sh
opencode plugin add opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@0.3.2 &&
  opencode plugin remove opencode-azure-devops-pr-review@PREVIOUS_VERSION
```

Run them when no AZPR command is running: OpenCode 2.1.4 switches the running
service to 0.3.2 within seconds, without a restart, and `opencode plugin list`
should then show a single `azpr` row with 0.3.2. Running only the first command
leaves the previous version running. For an entry with options, change only
its `package` value; the OpenCode service then downloads 0.3.2 with its own
network settings. See
[upgrading](https://github.com/WTLAIB/opencode-azure-devops-pr-review-v2/blob/v0.3.2/README.md#upgrading)
for the details. External settings, the PAT file and review records remain in
place, and this release adds no settings or required migration.

For a source installation, extract the new archive and run its installer with
`--replace` to retain settings:

```sh
sh install.sh --config-dir /absolute/path/to/v2-opencode-config --replace
```

## Compatibility and validation

The tested target remains OpenCode CLI **2.1.4** (V2 plugin API), Node.js
**22.23.3**, Ubuntu **22.04.5** under WSL2, and Azure DevOps Services REST API
**7.1**. OpenCode 1.x and Azure DevOps Server are not supported; other operating
systems remain unvalidated.
